title: The kingdom among you (Luke 17:20–37)
hook: the kingdom of God is within you, or in your midst

segments.voice: Yesterday, ten were healed and one returned, giving thanks. Your line was where are the nine? Who did you turn back to thank? Day five hundred sixty-four.

When? It's the question underneath a lot of religious life, in many times and places. When will things be put right? When will God act? People in Jesus' day had lived for generations under foreign rule, and they longed for the kingdom of God, the day God's reign would be plain to see. So some Pharisees ask him directly: when is it coming? It's a fair question, and he gets asked it more than once. His answer is just two verses long, and readers have argued about one tiny phrase in it for centuries.

In the King James Bible, he says: "The kingdom of God cometh not with observation: Neither shall they say, Lo here! or, lo there! for, behold, the kingdom of God is within you." Not with observation means you can't track it like an astronomer watching for a comet. Don't chase people who say it's over here, or over there. Then the tiny phrase. In Greek, entos hymon. It can mean within you, inside each person. That's how the King James reads it, and it gave Leo Tolstoy the title of a famous book. But it can also mean among you, in your midst. Many modern translations prefer that, partly because Jesus is speaking to people who were questioning him, and partly because of who was standing in front of them: Jesus himself. The kingdom is already here, in the middle of you, and you're asking when. Christians hold both readings. Some stress the inner life: God's reign begins in the heart. Others stress the community and the person of Jesus: God's reign is happening right here, among people, in what he's doing. Many say you need both. Then Jesus turns to his disciples and talks about the future: a day that will come as suddenly as lightning, while people are busy eating, drinking, marrying, planting, just as in the days of Noah and of Lot. Three words of warning: "Remember Lot's wife." She looked back. The whole passage holds two things together: the kingdom is already here, close enough to touch, and it is still coming. Don't spend your life peering at the horizon and miss what's in the room.
screen: then, large: `THE KINGDOM OF GOD IS WITHIN YOU.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: look for the kingdom in the room. Settle and breathe. Look around wherever you are. Notice the people near you, or the traces of people: a photo, a gift, the chair someone sat in. Where is there kindness here, patience, forgiveness, peace, even a small amount? Name one or two places. Then turn inward. Where in you is there something like that, a small good thing already growing? You don't have to manufacture it. Just notice it's there. If you pray, you can give thanks for it. The bell holds the time.
The kingdom among you. God's reign doesn't come with observation, Jesus says; it is within you, or in your midst, already here and still coming.
Your line: in your midst. Today, once every few hours, stop and look for one sign of the kingdom right where you are. Day five hundred sixty-four.

howItsDone: Christians pray thy kingdom come every time they say the Lord's Prayer, and many traditions speak of the kingdom as both already present and not yet complete, especially in Advent.

original.note: Greek: within you, or among you. a tiny phrase readers have argued about for centuries.

trapdoor: what you thought: the kingdom of God is a private feeling inside.
what it means: God's reign doesn't arrive by watching the horizon; it's already here, within and among people, and still coming.
what a scholar hears: entos hymon can mean within or among, and since Jesus was addressing questioners with himself standing there, many translators prefer in your midst.

notes: ἐντὸς ὑμῶν: 'within you' (KJV) vs 'among you / in your midst' (many modern versions). Reasons given are common in commentaries. Confirm.
'Three words of warning: Remember Lot's wife' is three words in the KJV. Confirm.
Tolstoy's book (1894) takes its title from this verse.
'Already and not yet' framing is broadly shared across churches; stated without ranking.
